gamma_events.title: Highest temperature in Munich on July 27?
gamma_events.description:
This market will resolve to the temperature range that contains the highest temperature recorded at the Munich Airport Station in degrees Celsius on 27 Jul '26.

The resolution source for this market will be information from Wunderground, specifically the highest temperature recorded for all times on this day for the Munich Airport Station, available here: https://www.wunderground.com/history/daily/de/munich/EDDM.

To toggle between Fahrenheit and Celsius, click the gear icon next to the search bar and switch the Temperature setting between °F and °C.

This market can not resolve until the first data point for the following date has been published on the resolution source.

The resolution source for this market measures temperatures to whole degrees Celsius (eg, 9°C). Thus, this is the level of precision that will be used when resolving the market.

Revisions to temperatures recorded within this market's timeframe will be considered until the first datapoint for the following date has been published, after which any alterations will not be considered.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent ensemble forecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and German Weather Service models indicate a peak temperature in Munich on July 27 most likely between 25°C and 26°C, reflecting modest uncertainty from variable cloud cover and weak northwesterly flow. These outcomes sit near the city's mid-July climatological average of 23–24°C, with differentiation among brackets driven by small shifts in daytime maximum timing, urban heat island contributions at official measurement sites, and any late-day convective development. Trader positioning remains closely balanced because short-range model runs continue to converge on this narrow band while longer-range guidance shows limited warming potential ahead of a possible frontal passage.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent Met Office guidance positions a 27°C maximum as the most probable outcome for London on July 27, citing high pressure and largely sunny conditions that limit cloud cover while preventing the stronger southerly flow seen during the earlier July heatwave. Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Forecast models from the National Weather Service and NOAA currently indicate a highest temperature in central NYC on July 26 near 81–84°F, with limited moisture and moderate onshore flow suppressing stronger daytime heating after the early-July heat wave. This consensus underpins the market’s tight clustering of implied probabilities around the low-to-mid 80s, where 82–83°F leads at 35.5% and 84–85°F follows at 25.5%. Recent ensemble guidance shows minimal spread, though small shifts in cloud cover or boundary-layer moisture could nudge readings a degree or two higher. Historical July climatology for the region centers near 84°F, providing context for why traders assign only modest odds to outcomes above 86°F. Updated model runs and afternoon observations tomorrow will refine these probabilities ahead of market resolution.

Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent Met Office guidance positions a 27°C maximum as the most probable outcome for London on July 27, citing high pressure and largely sunny conditions that limit cloud cover while preventing the stronger southerly flow seen during the earlier July heatwave. Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Forecast models from the National Weather Service and NOAA currently indicate a highest temperature in central NYC on July 26 near 81–84°F, with limited moisture and moderate onshore flow suppressing stronger daytime heating after the early-July heat wave. This consensus underpins the market’s tight clustering of implied probabilities around the low-to-mid 80s, where 82–83°F leads at 35.5% and 84–85°F follows at 25.5%. Recent ensemble guidance shows minimal spread, though small shifts in cloud cover or boundary-layer moisture could nudge readings a degree or two higher. Historical July climatology for the region centers near 84°F, providing context for why traders assign only modest odds to outcomes above 86°F. Updated model runs and afternoon observations tomorrow will refine these probabilities ahead of market resolution.

This market will resolve to the temperature range that contains the highest temperature recorded at the Tokyo Haneda Airport Station in degrees Celsius on 27 Jul '26.

The resolution source for this market will be information from Wunderground, specifically the highest temperature recorded for all times on this day for the Tokyo Haneda Airport Station, available here: https://www.wunderground.com/history/daily/jp/tokyo/RJTT.

This market can not resolve until the first data point for the following date has been published on the resolution source.

The resolution source for this market measures temperatures to whole degrees Celsius (eg, 9°C). Thus, this is the level of precision that will be used when resolving the market.

Revisions to temperatures recorded within this market's timeframe will be considered until the first datapoint for the following date has been published, after which any alterations will not be considered.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent Met Office guidance positions a 27°C maximum as the most probable outcome for London on July 27, citing high pressure and largely sunny conditions that limit cloud cover while preventing the stronger southerly flow seen during the earlier July heatwave. Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

Variability stems from uncertainty in the strength and position of the North Pacific subtropical high, which controls southerly flow and urban heat retention, alongside potential weak frontal influences or cloud cover that could moderate peaks. Historical July climatology shows typical maxima near 31°C with a standard deviation of 2–3°C, underscoring why small shifts in model guidance or observational updates can reweight outcomes. Traders are monitoring the next model cycles for clearer signals on these steering patterns ahead of resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent Met Office guidance positions a 27°C maximum as the most probable outcome for London on July 27, citing high pressure and largely sunny conditions that limit cloud cover while preventing the stronger southerly flow seen during the earlier July heatwave. Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

Variability stems from uncertainty in the strength and position of the North Pacific subtropical high, which controls southerly flow and urban heat retention, alongside potential weak frontal influences or cloud cover that could moderate peaks. Historical July climatology shows typical maxima near 31°C with a standard deviation of 2–3°C, underscoring why small shifts in model guidance or observational updates can reweight outcomes. Traders are monitoring the next model cycles for clearer signals on these steering patterns ahead of resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent Met Office guidance positions a 27°C maximum as the most probable outcome for London on July 27, citing high pressure and largely sunny conditions that limit cloud cover while preventing the stronger southerly flow seen during the earlier July heatwave. Ensemble forecasts show modest spread around this value, with some guidance reaching 28–29°C if daytime heating is enhanced by the urban heat island effect, while others settle near 26°C under slightly cooler northeasterly breezes. The summer’s 1.8°C above-average mean temperature has kept baseline warmth elevated, yet the post-heatwave cooling trend and stable ridge of high pressure support the market’s clustering around 26–28°C. Updated model runs and any Met Office briefing on July 26–27 will provide the clearest near-term signal for resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**High pressure building across southern England is driving trader consensus toward a peak of 32–33°C in London on July 29, with Met Office guidance indicating a maximum of 33°C under mostly sunny skies and light winds.** 

Recent model runs show warm southerly flow advecting air from the continent, supporting daytime highs several degrees above the July average of ~22–24°C, consistent with the ongoing warm spell across southeast England. Minor forecast spread arises from differences in predicted cloud cover timing, boundary-layer mixing, and the strength of the urban heat-island effect in central London, which can add 1–2°C locally. Official agencies such as the Met Office and ECMWF continue to converge on dry, stable conditions with little risk of significant cooling until later in the week, leaving the outcome sensitive to the final 24–48 hours of model updates. Traders therefore assign the highest implied probabilities to the narrow 32–34°C band while assigning low odds to extremes below 30°C or above 35°C.
